# The Silent Partner – Investment Appraisal with Taxes

> "The art of taxation consists in so plucking the goose as to obtain the largest amount of feathers with the least possible amount of hissing."
> — *Jean-Baptiste Colbert*

Chapters 5–7 assumed a perfect capital market — no frictions, no transaction costs, and no taxes. In reality, the state is a **silent partner** in every project: it claims a share of profits through corporate taxation (tax rate $s$), but simultaneously subsidises a share of financing costs through the tax deductibility of interest and depreciation.

This duality changes NPV arithmetic in two simultaneous and opposing directions. We use the **Standard Model of Corporate Taxation** (*Standardmodell nach Kruschwitz*) to integrate this partner precisely.

::: {.flip-card}
#### German Corporate Tax Rate
Germany's combined corporate tax burden runs approximately 30% — Körperschaftsteuer (15%), solidarity surcharge (0.825%), and Gewerbesteuer (trade tax, roughly 14%). The Standard Model uses a single rate $s$; calibrate it to the jurisdiction: US ~21%, UK ~25%, Ireland ~12.5%.
:::

## The Mechanism: Two Effects, Two Adjustments

Taxes act on two separate dimensions of the NPV formula simultaneously.

### Effect 1 — The Volume Effect: Adjusting Cash Flows

You pay taxes on **profit**, not on cash flow. Depreciation ($D_t$) reduces taxable profit but is not itself a cash outflow — so it saves you taxes without consuming cash.

$$\text{Tax payment} = s \cdot (CF_{before} - D_t)$$

$$\boxed{CF_{after} = CF_{before} \cdot (1-s) + D_t \cdot s}$$

The term $D_t \cdot s$ is the **Depreciation Tax Shield** — the cash taxes saved through depreciation write-offs. It raises after-tax cash flows and therefore acts on the **numerator** of the NPV formula.

::: {.flip-card}
#### Depreciation Tax Shield
Each euro of depreciation reduces taxable profit by one euro, saving $s$ euros in cash taxes. Firms prefer accelerated depreciation (*Sonderabschreibung*) because writing off assets earlier shifts tax savings forward in time — and earlier savings, discounted less heavily, have a higher present value.
:::

Reducing after-tax cash flows is the **Volume Effect**: taxes shrink the numerator of the NPV formula, reducing the project's value. This is the expected, intuitive direction.

### Effect 2 — The Interest Effect: Adjusting the Discount Rate

Interest payments on debt are **tax-deductible** (a business expense). Dividends are not (a distribution of after-tax profit). This asymmetry makes debt financing cheaper than its face rate suggests:

$$\boxed{i_{after} = i_{before} \cdot (1-s)}$$

If the bank charges 10% and the tax rate is 30%, the **effective** cost of capital is only 7%. The state covers the remaining 3% by forgoing the tax revenue it would otherwise receive on that interest income. This mechanism — the **Interest Tax Shield** — acts on the **denominator** of the NPV formula.

::: {.flip-card}
#### Interest Tax Shield vs. Depreciation Tax Shield
Both are "tax shields" but affect different parts of the NPV formula. The **Depreciation Tax Shield** ($D_t \cdot s$) reduces taxable income through asset write-offs, raising after-tax cash flows (numerator effect). The **Interest Tax Shield** ($i_{before} \cdot s$ per euro borrowed) makes debt financing cheaper, lowering the discount rate (denominator effect). The Standard Model captures both simultaneously.
:::

> **Financing assumption:** The formula $i_{after} = i_{before} \cdot (1-s)$ assumes projects are financed **entirely by debt at the margin** — every invested euro is borrowed. For mixed financing, use the Weighted Average Cost of Capital: $WACC = k_E \cdot \frac{E}{V} + k_D \cdot (1-s) \cdot \frac{D}{V}$, where the debt component carries the same $(1-s)$ adjustment.

::: {.drag-exercise}
In the Standard Model, taxes create two *opposing* forces: the *Volume Effect* shrinks after-tax *cash flows* (numerator), reducing NPV — while the *Interest Effect* lowers the *discount rate* (denominator), raising NPV.
:::

### A Complete Worked Example

**Project:** $I_0 = \text{€}\,100{,}000$, annual pre-tax CF = €\,30{,}000, straight-line depreciation over 5 years ($D_t = \text{€}\,20{,}000$/yr), $L_5 = 0$, pre-tax discount rate $i = 10\%$, tax rate $s = 30\%$.

**Adjusting the cash flows (Volume Effect):**
$$CF_{after} = 30{,}000 \times 0.70 + 20{,}000 \times 0.30 = 21{,}000 + 6{,}000 = \mathbf{\text{€}\,27{,}000}$$

**Adjusting the discount rate (Interest Effect):**
$$i_{after} = 10\% \times 0.70 = \mathbf{7\%}$$

**NPV before taxes** (pre-tax CF at $i = 10\%$):
$$NPV_{before} = -100{,}000 + 30{,}000 \times PVIFA(10\%,5) = -100{,}000 + 30{,}000 \times 3.7908 = \mathbf{+\text{€}\,13{,}724}$$

**NPV after taxes** (after-tax CF at $i_{after} = 7\%$):
$$NPV_{after} = -100{,}000 + 27{,}000 \times PVIFA(7\%,5) = -100{,}000 + 27{,}000 \times 4.1002 = \mathbf{+\text{€}\,10{,}705}$$

**Decomposing the tax impact of −€ 3,019:**

| Effect | Calculation | Value |
|:-------|:------------|------:|
| Volume Effect | $-3{,}000 \times 3.7908$ (lower CF at old rate) | −€ 11,372 |
| Interest Effect | $27{,}000 \times (4.1002 - 3.7908)$ (same CF at lower rate) | +€ 8,354 |
| **Net tax impact** | | **−€ 3,018** |

Here the Volume Effect dominates — taxes reduce the NPV by about € 3,000. But the Interest Effect recovers nearly three-quarters of the loss. Whether the Interest Effect can do even more — enough to turn a negative NPV positive — is the topic of the next section.

## The Lever: The Interest Tax Shield in Action

Why do private equity firms load their acquisitions with debt? Because in a world with taxes, a **levered firm** (with debt) is worth more than an otherwise identical **unlevered firm** (pure equity) — the government subsidises every euro of interest paid.

By reducing the denominator $i$, the present value of any given cash flow stream rises. The interactive tool below shows this lever across different tax rates and debt levels:

## The Anomaly: The Tax Paradox

The normal case: taxes destroy value — Volume Effect beats Interest Effect, $NPV_{after} < NPV_{before}$.

But the Standard Model has a mathematical twist. Under specific conditions, a project that is **unprofitable before taxes** becomes **profitable because of taxes**:

$$NPV_{before} < 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad NPV_{after} > 0$$

This is the **Tax Paradox** (*Steuerparadoxon*).

### The Tug-of-War

| Effect | Direction | Strength grows when… |
|:-------|:---------:|:---------------------|
| **Volume Effect** | ▼ reduces NPV | Tax rate $s$ is high |
| **Interest Effect** | ▲ raises NPV | Pre-tax rate $i$ is high; project life $n$ is long |

The paradox occurs when the **Interest Effect dominates** — which requires a sufficiently high pre-tax rate (a large tax shield base) combined with a long project life (many years over which the rate reduction compounds).

### A Numerical Example of the Paradox

**Project:** $I_0 = \text{€}\,100{,}000$, pre-tax CF = €\,27{,}000/yr, straight-line depreciation over 10 years ($D_t = \text{€}\,10{,}000$/yr), $n = 10$, pre-tax rate $i = 25\%$, tax rate $s = 40\%$.

**Before taxes** (at $i = 25\%$):
$$NPV_{before} = -100{,}000 + 27{,}000 \times PVIFA(25\%,10) = -100{,}000 + 27{,}000 \times 3.5705 = \mathbf{-\text{€}\,3{,}596}$$

The project fails — it destroys value before taxes.

**Adjusting for taxes** ($CF_{after} = 27{,}000 \times 0.60 + 10{,}000 \times 0.40 = \text{€}\,20{,}200$; $i_{after} = 25\% \times 0.60 = 15\%$):
$$NPV_{after} = -100{,}000 + 20{,}200 \times PVIFA(15\%,10) = -100{,}000 + 20{,}200 \times 5.0188 = \mathbf{+\text{€}\,1{,}380}$$

Taxes turned a loser into a winner. At 25% pre-tax, the Interest Tax Shield is enormous: it cuts the discount rate by 10 percentage points (25% → 15%), inflating the present value of every future cash flow far more than the Volume Effect deflates them.

::: {.details}
#### The Inflation Connection
The paradox becomes more likely under high inflation. Nominal interest rates rise with inflation, creating a larger Interest Tax Shield base. Meanwhile, the real value of future tax payments is eroded by inflation. Kruschwitz documented cases from post-war economies with double-digit nominal rates where the paradox surfaced routinely — firms profited from investing in otherwise marginal projects precisely because of their interest tax shields.
:::

## Strategic Levers: Playing the Tax Game

As a manager, you cannot change the tax laws. But you control two structural variables that determine which effect wins:

1. **Maximise debt** — until the bankruptcy risk outweighs the tax advantage. The optimal capital structure balances the Interest Tax Shield against distress costs (the Trade-Off Theory).
2. **Accelerate depreciation** — write off assets as fast as legally permitted. Depreciation in Year 1 saves taxes now; the same deduction in Year 5 saves taxes later. Earlier savings have a higher present value.

> **Management Rule:** "A tax deferred is a tax saved." Always postpone tax payments if legally permissible — the time value of the deferral creates real present value.

## Chapter Check

::: {.quick-check}
**How does the Standard Model adjust the discount rate to account for taxes?**

- It adds a risk premium.
- **It multiplies the pre-tax market rate by $(1 - s)$.**
- It leaves the rate unchanged.

> Correct. Interest on debt is tax-deductible, so the effective cost of debt financing is $i \times (1-s)$. The Standard Model assumes 100% debt financing at the margin; for mixed financing, use WACC with the $(1-s)$ factor applied to the debt component only.
:::

::: {.quick-check}
**When is the Tax Paradox most likely to occur?**

- When the discount rate is very low.
- **When the pre-tax discount rate is high and the project life is long.**
- When the company is already making a loss.

> Correct. A high pre-tax rate creates a large Interest Tax Shield base, and a long project life allows the rate reduction to compound across many periods. At i = 25% and n = 10, for example, the Interest Effect can easily dominate — converting a negative pre-tax NPV into a positive after-tax NPV.
:::

::: {.drag-exercise}
The *Tax Paradox* (*Steuerparadoxon*) occurs when the *Interest Effect* — the present-value gain from a lower *discount rate* — dominates the Volume Effect, so that a higher tax rate $s$ leads to a *higher* Net Present Value.
:::

Chapter 9 takes investment decisions beyond the single-project view: when capital is limited and multiple projects compete for the same budget, how does a firm rank and select the best combination — the Dean Model of capital rationing.
